mcqs.question: A product page's reviews service is down. Under graceful degradation, what should happen?
options: The entire page fails with an error, since one dependency is unavailable
The page waits indefinitely until the reviews service recovers
The page redirects the user to a maintenance page
The page shows the product and price normally, simply omitting the reviews section
mcqs.explanation: Graceful degradation means the core function (viewing and buying the product) survives even when a non-essential enhancement (reviews) is unavailable — that requires deciding in advance which parts are essential. Failing the whole page, waiting indefinitely, or redirecting all defeat the purpose of degrading gracefully.

mcqs.question: Why can deliberately rejecting some incoming requests (load shedding) improve overall system outcomes compared to accepting all of them?
options: It never actually improves outcomes; shedding always makes things strictly worse for users
Rejecting requests reduces the total revenue the system can ever generate
A system past capacity serving everyone badly (timeouts, retries, queuing) often delivers worse aggregate results than serving most requests well and shedding the rest fast
Shedding only matters for read requests, never affects write-heavy systems
mcqs.explanation: Past a capacity threshold, accepting every request tends to produce widespread timeouts and retries that make things worse for nearly everyone, while shedding some traffic early lets the rest be served well — a better aggregate outcome even though some requests are explicitly rejected. It applies to any overloaded system, not just reads, and it's about outcomes, not revenue directly.

mcqs.question: One specific internal service is saturated while the rest of the system is healthy. Where is shedding most precisely targeted?
options: At the edge/gateway only, since that's always the cheapest place to shed
Deep in the call chain, right at the saturated service, since that's where the real capacity limit is
Shedding can only happen at one layer in a system, never both
Nowhere — shedding only applies to overall system-wide overload, not a single service
mcqs.explanation: Shedding closest to the actual bottleneck targets the real capacity limit precisely, whereas edge shedding is coarse and doesn't know which internal service is saturated. The two layers aren't mutually exclusive, and shedding is equally valid for a single saturated service as for overall overload.

mcqs.question: A team assumes a failing non-critical dependency only affects its own feature. In practice the whole page errors out. What's the likely cause?
options: The response-building code has no path to catch that failure locally and substitute a fallback, so the exception propagates and fails the entire response
Non-critical dependencies always take down the whole system regardless of design
The dependency itself is critical, so this is expected behavior
The page's load balancer is misconfigured
mcqs.explanation: Without a designed fallback path, one failing call can throw an exception that isn't caught locally, taking the whole response down with it — that's a code-structure gap, not an inherent property of non-critical dependencies or the load balancer. Calling it "critical" contradicts the premise that it was meant to be non-critical.
